newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA INTERIM CABINET BOWS OUT, POPULARITY HIGH.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA INTERIM CABINET BOWS OUT, POPULARITY HIGH.

text.p: Bulgaria's interim government, handing over to its elected successor this week, has the rare distinction of leaving office as popular as when it came in.

In its three months in office it is credited with negotiating a $657 million accord with the International Monetary Fund, stabilising the national currency, and bringing grain and fuel shortages under control.

Interim Prime Minister Stefan Sofianski, who delivered his cabinet's final report to President Petar Stoyanov on Tuesday, said he was proud of having helped Bulgarians to survive the worst of the crisis and wished success to the new team to be presented to parliament on Wednesday.
"I hope the new cabinet will have the same support from society as we did because relying only on support from the political forces it won't be able to cope," he told reporters.
Tuesday's Novinar daily published an article headlined "99 days which changed Bulgaria", saying Sofianski was the first premier to leave office with such a high approval rating.

Prime minister designate Ivan Kostov, leader of the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) which won last month's election, on Tuesday presented his cabinet and its programme to Stoyanov and said he would continue reforms started by Sofianski's cabinet.

Kostov is keeping on five ministers from the interim cabinet, including deputy premier and industry minister Alexander Bozhkov and interior minister Bogomil Bonev who will continue his campaign against crime and high-level corruption.
His cabinet includes Muravei Radev, 50, head of the previous parliament's economic commission, as finance minister, and UDF deputy leader Nadezhda Mihailova as foreign minister.

The main priorities outlined in the UDF programme are carrying out economic reform, making provision for its social cost, fighting organised crime, opening secret police files of public figures, returning land to its pre-communist owners and bringing Bulgaria into the European Union and NATO.
By the end of July parliament is expected to pass the delayed 1997 budget, and laws for introduction of a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime, the IMF-prescribed currency board.
The UDF has 137 seats in the 240-seat parliament, compared to 58 for the former ruling Socialists, widely blamed by Bulgarians for the country's economic near-collapse.

The UDF has strong support from the small Euroleft coalition which includes prominent Socialist dissidents, and more guarded support from the Union for National Salvation, which includes ethnic Turks and monarchists.
Vassil Gotsev, justice minister in the new cabinet and a leading UDF member, said he hoped for broad political support from the new parliament.
"We rely on the support of all parliamentary forces despite the Socialists as we are suggesting a reasonable programme to end the crisis and a good team to implement it," he said.
